# Maximizing EBS HDD Performance

Contributors: [Kadir Ozdemir](mailto:kozdemir@salesforce.com), [Ashutosh Parekh](mailto:ashutosh.parekh@salesforce.com), [Gourab Taparia](mailto:gtaparia@salesforce.com)  
Updated: May 15, 2024

EBS HDD (st1) volumes are throughput optimized volumes to provide low-cost magnetic storage. This volume type is a good fit for large, sequential workloads. These volumes provide impressive  throughput at low cost.  However, to achieve maximum throughput on these volumes, the I/O requests sent to these volumes has to be 1MiB. 

In this document, we explain the I/O stack on EBS volumes and analyze their performance characteristics. Then we explain the HBase I/O path for Argus and Core workloads and provide currently achieved per volume throughput for them. Finally, we make recommendations on how to achieve maximum throughput.

# EBS HDD Volume Performance Characteristics

The [specification](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/hdd-vols.html) provided for EBS HDD volumes includes only their baseline and max throughput but does not specify IOPS for them. Without knowing IOPS, it is not easy to calculate the expected throughput for different I/O sizes. 

A recent AWS knowledge center [post](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/ebs-low-throughput-performance) on EBS HDD volumes implies that IOPS for a given volume equals to baseline throughput divided by 1 MiB. For example, a 4TB volume provides 160 MiB/s throughput. For this volume, IOPS would be 160 IO/s. We have verified this with various performance tests. Before going into details of the implications of this, we need to explain the typical I/O stack depicted in the following diagram.

A block device can be thought of as a contiguous space of fixed sized blocks. The typical size of a block is 4KB but the size is configurable. Each block is referenced by an address called Logical Block Address (LBA) by the application using the block device directly. For example, the file system created on the block device uses LBA to refer to blocks. Please note the mapping from a file to the blocks of the underlying block device is maintained by the file system. The corresponding physical blocks of the device can also be thought of as sequentially laid out on their physical media in the order of their LBAs. 

When a sequential chunk of blocks of an HDD device corresponding to an I/O request is accessed, the access time for the first block dominates the total operation time for this request which is typically in single digit milliseconds. Then reading or writing the subsequent blocks is done in microseconds. This is the reason HDD devices are good fit for sequential workloads but not for random workloads. The number of I/O operations is typically fixed and limited on these devices regardless of the I/O size. That is why using larger I/O requests gives better throughput. 

The I/O scheduler layer in the kernel of an OS first places the I/O requests for a block device on the queue allocated for this device. The IO requests are then sorted and merged based on their LBAs to maximize the throughput of the device by the I/O scheduler. 

As being a block device, EBS HDD volumes behave similarly to other HDD devices.   
EBS volumes are not locally attached devices. They are accessed over a storage network. In AWS, there are separate network cards in EC2 instances for networked attached storage devices. These cards are called [Nitro](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/nitro/#:~:text=The%20AWS%20Nitro%20System%20is,re%2Dimagined%20our%20virtualization%20infrastructure.) cards.  

There are two parameters in Linux that determine the maximum size of an I/O request to a block device. These are 

* max\_hw\_sectors\_kb: This is the maximum number of kilobytes supported in a single data transfer by the underlying device. This value is read-only. It is set by the driver to reflect the driver/hardware limit.   
* max\_sectors\_kb: This is the maximum number of kilobytes that the block layer will allow for a file system request. This is a configurable parameter.

The block layer in Linux takes the minimum of these two parameters to determine the maximum I/O size for a given block device. EBS block devices set max\_hw\_sectors\_kb to 256 KiB.  However, EBS block devices merge smaller I/O requests larger than 32KiB into 1MiB requests if they are sequential in Nitro cards.  This merging happens at the client side by the firmware of Nitro. Maximum I/O merging (and thus maximum throughput with I/O smaller than 1 MiB and larger than or equal to 32 KiB) is obtained on a volume only by

* a single stream of sequential I/O (either read or write) requests, or  
* a single stream of sequential reads plus a single stream of sequential writes

These volumes always use 1 MiB I/O tokens regardless of the actual I/O size that is used by the workload on the EC2 instance. There are two merge tokens per volume, one for read requests and the other for write requests. If the actual I/O size received by the EBS volume is 16 KiB, then the volume still uses the entire 1024 KiB size of the I/O token. Doing this wastes most of the token's space. To maximize efficiency, the entire 1 MiB token needs to fill.

When the I/O size of a sequential workload is greater than 32 KiB, Amazon EBS always merges the I/Os into a single I/O operation of 1 MiB. This merging fills the entire token size.

When the I/O size is smaller than 32 KiB or if the workload is random, Amazon EBS does not merge the I/Os to 1 MiB. However, Amazon EBS still uses the entire 1 MiB token size. This leaves most of the space inside the token empty. Because the I/Os aren't merged, the instance uses more IOPS to send the same amount of data to the volume. This reduces the burst balance even though the throughput is less than its baseline value.

## FIO Testing

The following FIO tests are executed on a single 6TB EBS st1 volume (with 240 MiB/s baseline throughput).

The following table shows that EBS does not merge I/O requests less than 32KiB. 

| Test | I/O Size | Read Throughput | Write Throughput |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Single Sequential Stream  | 16 KiB | 8.3 MiB/s | 8.3 MiB/s |
|  | 32 KiB | 161 MiB/s | 527 MiB/s |
|  | 64 KiB | 276 MiB/s | 530 MiB/s |
|  | 1 MiB | 533 MiB/s | 533 MiB/s |

The following tests show that random I/O cannot be merged. When 1MiB requests are used, maximum throughput is achieved.

| Test | I/O Size | Read Throughput | Write Throughput |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Single Random Stream | 16 KiB | 8.3 MiB/s | 8.2 MiB/s |
|  | 32 KiB | 16.7 MiB/s | 16.5 MiB/s |
|  | 64 KiB | 33.4 MiB/s | 33.1 MiB/s |
|  | 1 MiB | 533 MiB/s | 533 MiB/s  |

The tests on the table below are done with multiple sequential I/O streams. As can be seen from these tests, multiple streams of read or multiple streams of write drastically reduce the throughput when the I/O size is less than 1MB.

| Test | I/O Size | Throughput |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 sequential read stream \+ 1 sequential write stream | 64 KiB | 479 MiB/s 229 MiB/s (Read) \+ 250 MiB/s (Write) |
| 3 sequential read streams |  | 111 MiB/s |
| 6 sequential read streams |  | 86 MiB/s |
| 6 sequential read streams \+ 1 sequential write stream |  | 98.7 MiB/s 81.2 MiB/s (Read) \+17.5 MiB/s (Write) |
| 1 random read stream \+ 1 sequential write stream |  | 63.5 MiB/s 31.3 MiB/s (Read) \+ 32.2 MiB/s (Write) |
| 1 random read stream \+ 1 sequential write stream | 1 MiB | 520 MiB/s 233 MiB/s (Read) \+ 287 MiB/s (Write) |
| 6 sequential read streams \+ 1 sequential write stream |  | 314 MiB/s 265 MiB/s (Read) \+ 49.6 MiB/s (Write) |

# EBS Volume Throughput in Production

HBase is a log structured merge-tree (LSM tree) based data storage such that writes are written a log called WAL (*Write Ahead Log*) sequentially while buffered in memory (commonly referred as *memstore*). When buffered data in memstore reaches a certain size, it is flushed to disk. This buffered data is also written sequentially. 

HBase reads its files called *HFiles* block by block and currently HBase block size is set to 64 KiB in production. HBase provides two types of read operation, scan and get. The scan operation is for scanning a section of a table or the entire table. Scan operations also lead to reading blocks from the disk sequentially. A get operation (which is a scan for reading one row) is a point lookup operation and may lead to accessing HBase blocks randomly.

There are two main types of workloads for HBase clusters in Production today. These are core (NOSQL database) and Argus (time series database) workload. In the core workload, read operations include both point lookups and range scans. The MapReduce jobs for background operations usually generate full table scans.  In the Argus workload, only range scans are used as Argus is a time series database.

Although the workload on EBS volumes generated by the HBase clusters is mostly sequential, the per volume achieved throughput is a fraction of the baseline throughput as can be seen from the table given above. 

As explained in the previous section, EBS HDD volume throughput can be maximized only when the I/O size is 1 MiB or the I/Os that are larger than or equals to 32 KiB and they are sequential (that is they can be merged into 1MiB I/Os). When there are multiple read or write I/O streams, then merging happens less frequently. 

Even if both read and write operations are sequential but use I/O much smaller than 1MiB and there are multiple streams of read and/or write operations on a single volume, the aggregated workload from these streams will behave like a random workload and reduce the overall throughput. This is the reason for the current low volume-throughput utilization in production. Let us explain this now. To do that, we need to briefly explain the I/O path for HBase.

Read and write operations are processed by the server nodes called *region servers* in HBase. HBase uses HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) files for its backing store.  In HDFS, file read and write requests are handled by the server nodes called *data nodes*. The number of EBS volumes attached to each data node is 6 currently. HDFS is designed for large files and it uses large blocks to store its files. The block size for HDFS is set to 128 MiB in production. These blocks are stored as individual files in local file systems created over EBS volumes. Read and write operations on HDFS files are translated into read and write operations on these local file system files. 

Read and write operations on HBase region servers are done using RPC operations. HBase uses a separate thread to handle each of these operations. These threads are referred to as *handlers*. Currently running (i.e., active) threads are called *active handlers*. The number of active handlers can be as high as 256 currently.

Each cluster can come with a different number of region servers and data nodes. For Agus clusters, the ratio of the number of region servers to the number of data nodes is around 3\. For core clusters, this ratio is around ½. This means that the number of volumes per region server is around 2 for Argus and 12 for core. Since the number of active handlers per region server is certainly much higher than the number of volumes per region server, a single EBS volume will receive I/O from multiple streams concurrently from region servers. And this will cause low volume-throughput utilization.

We have explained that even if each I/O operation results in a sequential stream of I/O requests (much smaller than 1 MiB, for example, 64 KiB), a high number of such concurrent streams will cause low throughput utilization. It is worth noting that HBase is not the only cluster with high number concurrent streams, Kafka is another cluster.

We need to note that even though the number of volumes per region server in core is much higher than that in Argus, the throughput utilization between these workloads is not really very different. This is because core workload includes random point lookups in addition to range scans.

Given that after merge average write I/O size is 210KiB, before merge average write I/O size is roughly 160KiB. Seeing more merges for writes are expected as WAL, memstore flush, and compaction writes in HBase are supposed to sequential workload. The reason that we do not see them merged more than 30% is because the size of the I/O generated by the HBase is already large for the EBS block driver as the maximum I/O size accepted by the EBS block driver is 256KiB.  
![][image5]

Using the above data collected production data, we can model the I/O workload on a given disk and estimate per EBS volume performance. The number of DNs per RS is roughly 2 for core clusters. Each DN has 6 2TB volumes. This means that there are 12 disks to be used for WAL writes per RS. Each WAL file will be replicated 3 times, so a given RS would only use 3 EBS volumes for its WAL writes. Thus only ¼ of the volumes will be used for WAL writes. This means the number of WAL write streams on disk would not be more than one. In addition to the WAL writes, EBS volumes get writes from memstore flushes and compaction. We will consider that a given EBS volume receives sequential write workload and but random read workload.   
To simulate, the prod5 core cluster workload on an EBS volumes, we run a FIO test with one sequential write job and one random read job where the write I/O size is between 190KiB and 220KiB and the read I/O size is between 100KiB and 160KiB. In this test, we used a 2TB volume and one 100GB file for each read and write job. The test ran for 10 minutes. Just before running the above test, we run another FIO test to deplete the EBS volume burst balance for two hours. This test used 1MiB read I/O. This test resulted in 10MiB/s read throughput and 0.5MiB write throughput. This throughput is not less than the per volume throughput we observe in production. The baseline throughput for an EBS volume is 80MiB/s and this FIO test achieved about 13% throughput utilization. Please note our production cluster achieves even lower throughput utilization.

Using the same model, we can estimate the throughput improvement we will obtain if HBase generates 1MiB read and write I/O in production. So we run the same FIO test using 1MiB IO size. Again before running the actual FIO test, we ran the random read FIO test for two hours to deplete the EBS volume burst balance. 1MiB I/O size resulted in 35.5MiB/s read throughput and 45.0MiB/s write throughput. The expected improvement in throughput would be 9X for writes and 3.5X for reads.

# How To Maximize Volume Throughput

From the previous section, in order to achieve maximum throughput, we conclude that either the application needs to directly generates a workload of 1 MiB I/O requests or the I/O request generated by the application needs to be higher than or equal to 32 KiB and sequential for a given volume so that they can be merged into larger I/O requests. In order to maximize I/O merging, the number of sequential streams needs to be minimized. For maximum merging, a volume can have at most one write and one read stream.

In the following sections, we describe how to increase the throughput for Argus and core workloads.

## Argus

For Argus, it is very likely we can set HBase block size to 1 MiB. This will ensure that memstore flushes and scan will use 1 MiB I/O requests. 

The size of I/O requests generated by WAL is determined by how frequently the WAL write records are flushed to the disk. The WAL records are sequentially laid out on the WAL file. As explained before, the write operations from HBase clients are done through RPCs. The write operations from RPC handlers are then added to a ring buffer for the WAL file and this ring buffer is flushed to disk using a separate set of threads called SyncRunners. The number of SyncRunners is currently 5\. The reason that there are multiple SyncRunners is to reduce the write latency. Argus uses an asynchronous client so increasing the latency of writes by 5 times by using only one SyncRunner would not be a concern. This will increase the average WAL write I/O size by up to 5 times. 

Using smaller volumes (2TB volumes) but more volumes will also help as WAL write requests can be still less than 1 MiB even after using a single SyncRunner per region server. Also, increasing the write batch size used by the Argus client would help. 

## Core

For core, it is very unlikely we can set HBase block size to 1 MiB at the cluster level. This is because the queries for some tables can be mostly point lookups and using 1 MiB block for point lookups will pollute the HBase block cache and reduce its efficiency. However, we can configure different block sizes for different tables instead of configuring the same block size for all. There will be tables for which we can set block sizes larger than 64 KiB will help. For others, using 32KiB could be even better (for example Vagabond use case can benefit from this).

To improve the read performance in general, we need to increase the number of volumes per region server. Currently, core uses 2TB volumes. We can reduce the volume size to 1TB and double the number of volumes. If the workload consisted of just sequential streams, then setting the number of volumes to the number of streams would give us the best throughput. However, having random point lookup streams like the ones in the core workload will not allow us to achieve baseline throughput. At some point, increasing the number of volumes will not help. Actually, it may increase the latency for individual point lookups and thus we may not be able to reduce the volume size further. Please note that when we improve the throughput, we should see that the latency for our queries will improve too in general. So, it is expected that going from 2TB to 1TB should both improve throughput and latency. Further reducing volume size may not improve the overall cluster performance.

Reducing the number of SyncRunners to 1 will also improve the throughput for the core workload. This change along with the above mentioned changes should not cause any significant increase in average write latency clients experience as this will improve the overall cluster throughput as well as the WAL throughput. Since WAL and HFiles share the same set of volumes, any improvement in the access patterns will improve both throughput and latency.
